title: Why America needs the CLARITY Act
gist: Andreessen and Dixon argue the CLARITY Act (the Senate market-structure bill covering the 85% of crypto not addressed by the GENIUS Act) is the difference between a permanently regulated, U.S.-led crypto/stablecoin industry and a continuation of regulatory gray-area 'anarcho-tyranny' that produces more FTX-style blowups and cedes the technology to less accountable offshore actors.

insights.claim: Stablecoin transaction volume now rivals the size of the Visa network, with trillions of dollars per quarter moving through the system.
insights.speaker: a16z crypto editorial
insights.so_what: Confirms stablecoins have crossed from experimental to systemically significant payment volume, which is the underlying reason regulators/banks are now forced to engage.
insights.quote: Stablecoin volume now rivals the size of the Visa network.
insights.locator: Chris: As Marc was saying, way back in 2014

insights.claim: Major institutions including BlackRock, JPMorgan, Visa, Fidelity, and Mastercard have all rushed to build on crypto/blockchain infrastructure despite the absence of comprehensive federal rules.
insights.speaker: a16z crypto editorial
insights.so_what: Institutional adoption is already ahead of regulation, meaning any regulatory resolution (positive or negative) has an unusually large addressable base of incumbents ready to scale.
insights.locator: Robert: You cited that stablecoin volumes are now rivaling the Visa network

insights.claim: On-chain transaction costs and speed have improved dramatically: what cost a couple to tens of dollars per transaction three years ago now settles in under one second for less than a penny on chains like Solana and Ethereum.
insights.speaker: a16z crypto editorial
insights.so_what: A Moore's-law-like cost/latency curve on blockchains is the enabling condition for consumer-scale payments use cases (e.g., remittances), independent of the regulatory outcome.
insights.quote: That’s due to the equivalent of Moore’s law on blockchains: you’ve gotten more and more performant chains.
insights.locator: Even three years ago, what I just described might cost

insights.claim: The base layer chains (Bitcoin, Ethereum) have never been hacked; publicized crypto hacks have been the result of lax security at organizations using them, not chain-level compromise.
insights.speaker: a16z crypto editorial
insights.so_what: Reframes crypto hack headlines as an operational/counterparty risk issue rather than a protocol risk issue — relevant when assessing exchange vs. base-layer investment risk.
insights.quote: Bitcoin has never been hacked. Ethereum has never been hacked.
insights.locator: You read about hacks and things in the newspaper

insights.claim: Crypto regulation was split for political reasons into stablecoins (~15% of market cap) covered by the GENIUS Act, and the remaining ~85% of the market (blockchains and other tokens) still lacking a federal framework, which the CLARITY Act is meant to address.
insights.speaker: a16z crypto editorial
insights.so_what: Quantifies exactly how much of the crypto market remains regulatorily exposed, framing CLARITY as closing the dominant, not marginal, gap.
insights.quote: Stablecoins are roughly 15 percent of the market, let’s call it, and the rest is 85 percent.
insights.locator: For political and policy reasons, regulation around crypto

insights.claim: The GENIUS Act's stablecoin framework requires full dollar-for-dollar backing held in audited bank accounts and short-term Treasuries, directly preventing an FTX- or Terra-Luna-style shortfall.
insights.speaker: a16z crypto editorial
insights.so_what: Explains the specific regulatory mechanism (segregated, audited, T-bill-backed reserves) that de-risks compliant stablecoins for institutional adoption — a template CLARITY extends to the rest of the market.
insights.quote: If you’re an American consumer and you use USDC or another GENIUS-compliant stablecoin... there is a dollar sitting in the bank, because that’s the GENIUS regulation.
insights.locator: Last year, a bill passed Congress

insights.claim: Regulatory clarity itself, not just underlying technology, is credited as the direct cause of stablecoins' takeoff over the past year — builders gained certainty and consumers gained trust once GENIUS passed.
insights.speaker: a16z crypto editorial
insights.so_what: Suggests CLARITY passage could similarly unlock adoption in tokenized securities, lending, and other non-stablecoin segments currently gated by ambiguity.
insights.quote: It’s not a coincidence that stablecoins are also the area that has taken off the most in the last year, because once you have regulatory clarity, builders have certainty and consumers know what to expect.
insights.locator: Last year, a bill passed Congress and was signed by the president

insights.claim: The current situation is analogous to regulating cellphones but not cell towers: stablecoins (the application layer) are regulated while the underlying blockchains and broader token market (the infrastructure layer) are not.
insights.speaker: a16z crypto editorial
insights.so_what: A memorable framing investors can use to explain to non-crypto-native stakeholders why partial (GENIUS-only) regulation is insufficient for full institutional confidence.
insights.quote: You can imagine it as if we had a regulatory framework for cellphones, but not for cell towers.
insights.locator: But the big hanging problem right now is this other section

themes.theme: History: from Bitcoin op-ed to mature industry

insights.claim: Andreessen's 2014 New York Times op-ed 'Why Bitcoin Matters' is framed as having held up well on the thesis that adoption was still early, but wrong in scope — it should have said 'crypto' broadly rather than 'Bitcoin' specifically, since the industry fragmented into many blockchains and platforms (Ethereum and beyond) rather than extending Bitcoin itself via proposals like 'colored coins.'
insights.speaker: a16z crypto editorial
insights.so_what: Illustrates a durable pattern for tech forecasting: correct on adoption-curve timing, wrong on which specific implementation wins — useful heuristic for evaluating current crypto/AI infrastructure bets.
insights.quote: I think the thing that, in retrospect, needs to be changed about the piece is: every time I said Bitcoin, just swap in crypto.
insights.locator: Marc: Sure. 2014 was so long ago

insights.claim: Crypto has moved from a 'cultish subculture of hobbyists' circa 2014 to a mature industry where major banks and fintechs announce stablecoin, tokenized-stock, and digital-asset platforms daily.
insights.speaker: a16z crypto editorial
insights.so_what: Signals the investable universe has shifted from speculative retail assets to institutional infrastructure plays.
insights.locator: Chris: As Marc was saying, way back in 2014

themes.theme: FTX, Terra-Luna, and the case for a federal crypto regulator

insights.claim: There is currently no federal regulator for crypto exchanges (unlike the NYSE and Nasdaq), which the CLARITY Act would fix by giving the SEC and CFTC oversight, disclosure regimes, anti-fraud rules, and insider-trading rules.
insights.speaker: a16z crypto editorial
insights.so_what: Identifies the specific structural gap (no exchange-level federal regulator) that CLARITY closes — a concrete diligence checkpoint for evaluating exchange counterparty risk pre- vs. post-passage.
insights.quote: Right now, there is no federal regulator for crypto exchanges, as an example.
insights.locator: Chris: Right now, there is no federal regulator

insights.claim: Terra-Luna failed because it was a self-referential stablecoin whose value depended on its own token rather than being backed by dollars or other stable assets; this structure would be illegal under the GENIUS framework.
insights.speaker: a16z crypto editorial
insights.so_what: Gives investors a concrete red-flag pattern (self-referential/algorithmic backing) to screen out in future stablecoin-like products, now reinforced by law.
insights.quote: It was essentially a self-referential thing in which the token’s value depended on the token itself.
insights.locator: Another big catastrophe was Terra-Luna

insights.claim: The 2020–2024 U.S. administration pursued a prosecutorial rather than regulatory approach to crypto, and the resulting five-year vacuum pushed activity offshore into jurisdictions with weaker controls, culminating in the FTX collapse.
insights.speaker: a16z crypto editorial
insights.so_what: Frames FTX not as an indictment of crypto itself but as a predictable consequence of regulatory abdication — supports the thesis that clear rules reduce blowup risk rather than merely constraining growth.
insights.quote: The real answer is you can’t trust fully unregulated crypto.
insights.locator: That culminated in the catastrophe of FTX

insights.claim: The historical precedent cited for why federal securities-style regulation benefits an industry is the Securities Acts that created the SEC, after which U.S. capital markets became globally dominant for the following 90-100 years.
insights.speaker: a16z crypto editorial
insights.so_what: Historical analog investors can use to gauge the multi-decade upside case a16z is making for crypto market structure legislation.
insights.locator: The most famous case is the Securities Acts

insights.claim: Regulatory ambiguity creates a 'race to the bottom': for every compliant U.S. company like Coinbase, an offshore 'evil twin' emerges that copies the product, skips compliance costs, and wins market share on price and speed.
insights.speaker: a16z crypto editorial
insights.so_what: Explains the competitive-dynamics mechanism by which unclear rules structurally favor bad actors over compliant incumbents — a reason institutional investors should prefer clear-perimeter regulation even if it raises compliance costs.
insights.quote: The ambiguity ends up favoring the bad actors.
insights.locator: Every year, a new offshore competitor pops up

insights.claim: National-security officials reportedly prefer criminals and terrorists use crypto over legacy systems because blockchain transactions leave a permanent, traceable trail, unlike systems such as hawala.
insights.speaker: a16z crypto editorial
insights.so_what: Directly counters the Elizabeth Warren-style 'sanctions evasion' critique of CLARITY with an insider claim that traceability, not anonymity, is crypto's defining property for law enforcement — worth weighing against political risk to the bill.
insights.quote: Ironically, they’re hoping more criminals and terrorists use crypto and blockchains because there’s a trail.
insights.locator: Marc: I’ve spent quite a lot of time in the national-security world

insights.claim: The hawala system — an informal, centuries-old peer-to-peer payment network with no digital or paper trail and no physical cash movement across borders — is cited as a primary channel financing Middle Eastern terror plots today, and is untraceable in ways crypto is not.
insights.speaker: a16z crypto editorial
insights.so_what: Provides a concrete comparison point that undercuts the 'crypto enables terror financing' argument by naming the actually-untraceable incumbent system.
insights.quote: There’s no digital trail because nothing has happened digitally. No paper trail, nothing.
insights.locator: I’ll give you an example from the world of Middle Eastern terrorism

insights.claim: National-security circles previously used the term 'prosecution futures' to describe the strategic value of criminals moving to crypto, since it lets law enforcement mine the blockchain to prosecute them later.
insights.speaker: a16z crypto editorial
insights.so_what: A specific insider term-of-art that, if accurate, signals law enforcement views crypto adoption by bad actors as net favorable for eventual prosecution, relevant to policy risk assessment on illicit-finance objections.
insights.quote: They called crypto ‘prosecution futures’: if we could get the bad guys to use crypto instead of other methods, we would be able to mine the blockchain to prosecute down the road.
insights.locator: There was a term national-security people were kicking around

insights.claim: Building privacy into public blockchains is described as a nontrivial, unsolved research and product-development problem, motivated by legitimate use cases (e.g., private medical or financial payments) rather than criminality, drawing a direct parallel to Netscape's invention of SSL/HTTPS.
insights.speaker: a16z crypto editorial
insights.so_what: Flags on-chain privacy tooling as an open technical frontier and investable gap — a recurring theme where blockchain's default transparency is now seen as a liability needing product solutions.
insights.quote: It’s actually a nontrivial research and product-development problem to build blockchains that have privacy, because they are so public.
insights.locator: Chris: It’s actually a nontrivial research and product-development problem

insights.claim: Netscape had to ship a deliberately weakened, export-labeled version of its browser overseas for four years under ITAR export-control rules that classified strong encryption as a munition equivalent to a Tomahawk missile, which caused foreign competitors to win overseas share with unrestricted strong encryption until the policy was reversed.
insights.speaker: a16z crypto editorial
insights.so_what: A direct historical precedent a16z uses to argue that restrictive tech policy costs American companies global market share to foreign competitors — the explicit analogy being drawn to today's crypto and AI liability debates.
insights.quote: Encryption was classified in the same category as a Tomahawk missile, which meant the Netscape browser was classified in the same category as a Tomahawk missile.
insights.locator: Marc: It was a four-year fight

insights.claim: After the ITAR/encryption fight resolved, American internet industry ended up dominating globally, and national-security agencies came to prefer dealing with American companies over ones based in other jurisdictions.
insights.speaker: a16z crypto editorial
insights.so_what: Reinforces the article's core policy argument: permissive, clear tech regulation at home strengthens rather than weakens national security by keeping dominant platforms US-based and accountable.
insights.quote: If you’re in the national-security state and you ask whether you’d rather have this giant industry dominated by American or non-American companies, 100 percent of the time they’ll tell you they want it dominated by American companies.
insights.locator: The other incredibly positive thing that happened

insights.claim: Senator Elizabeth Warren has publicly opposed the CLARITY Act, calling it a 'ticket to sanctions evasion' and warning it would let North Korea, terrorists, and ransomware hackers 'run wild.'
insights.speaker: a16z crypto editorial
insights.so_what: Identifies the specific named political opposition and framing risk investors should track as a signal for bill passage odds.
insights.quote: She and her camp have called it a ticket to sanctions evasion.
insights.locator: In fact, one of the biggest opponents to the bill

insights.claim: The Fraternal Order of Police, the largest law-enforcement organization in the country, has endorsed the CLARITY Act, cited as evidence against claims the bill lacks anti-money-laundering and sanctions safeguards.
insights.speaker: a16z crypto editorial
insights.so_what: A concrete, checkable endorsement signal that political support for CLARITY spans beyond the crypto industry into law enforcement — relevant for gauging passage likelihood.
insights.quote: The Fraternal Order of Police just came out with its endorsement of the CLARITY Act, the largest law-enforcement organization in the country.
insights.locator: This is simply not true. It has strict definitions

insights.claim: Government ethics provisions tied to crypto have become a sticking point because the bill couples industry market-structure regulation with government-official ethics rules for the first time in U.S. history, and the president's family crypto interests are cited by critics as a conflict of interest.
insights.speaker: a16z crypto editorial
insights.so_what: Identifies a distinct, still-unresolved political risk factor (ethics negotiation) separate from the substantive market-structure debate that could independently delay or sink the bill.
insights.quote: This bill, as proposed right now, would be the first bill in U.S. history, I’m told, that regulates an industry and also adds specific ethics provisions for government officials.
insights.locator: Point number three: what has been frustrating from a political point of view

insights.claim: The CLARITY Act as drafted imposes stronger restrictions on government officials' crypto holdings (disclosure requirements, lockups) than currently exist for officials' stock trading.
insights.speaker: a16z crypto editorial
insights.so_what: A specific rebuttal data point to the 'bill enriches insiders' criticism, useful for assessing the actual conflict-of-interest exposure rather than the political narrative.
insights.quote: This bill puts controls on government officials’ use of crypto that are stronger than those that apply to government officials’ stock trading.
insights.locator: Marc: This bill puts controls on government officials’ use of crypto

insights.claim: JPMorgan Chase has been the most vocal banking-lobby opponent of allowing interest to be paid on stablecoin holdings, fearing deposit flight from banks if consumers can earn yield on stablecoins instead.
insights.speaker: a16z crypto editorial
insights.so_what: Names the specific incumbent and mechanism (deposit-flight fear) driving the most consequential compromise in the bill — a direct read on where bank-vs-fintech lobbying tension will keep recurring post-passage.
insights.locator: You mentioned stablecoins again. One of the big fights

insights.claim: The bill's compromise bans paying interest on stablecoin balances (or anything functionally/economically similar to a bank account), but permits transaction-based rewards programs (e.g., a merchant rewarding repeat stablecoin wallet use), similar to credit-card rewards.
insights.speaker: a16z crypto editorial
insights.so_what: Precisely defines the legal boundary between prohibited stablecoin 'interest' and permitted 'rewards' — a structuring detail relevant to any fintech/stablecoin product design post-CLARITY.
insights.quote: You can give them rewards for using their stablecoin wallet twice a month at Walmart.
insights.locator: What you can do is something more complicated

insights.claim: The stablecoin-interest debate is publicly embodied by a rivalry between Coinbase CEO Brian Armstrong and JPMorgan CEO Jamie Dimon, even though JPMorgan itself runs a large blockchain unit with live tokenized deposits on-chain.
insights.speaker: a16z crypto editorial
insights.so_what: Highlights the contradiction of an incumbent bank simultaneously lobbying to slow crypto regulation while building competing blockchain products — a signal that large banks are hedging both sides of the transition.
insights.quote: It’s interesting that they’re trying to slow-roll CLARITY while also building on this technology.
insights.locator: Robert: The thing I find so interesting

insights.claim: Goldman Sachs CEO David Solomon has publicly endorsed the CLARITY Act, alongside Fidelity, BlackRock and other major financial institutions.
insights.speaker: a16z crypto editorial
insights.so_what: Concrete, trackable list of institutional endorsers that signals broadening Wall Street buy-in beyond crypto-native firms — a bullish tell for passage odds and for institutional capital rotating into the space.
insights.quote: Goldman Sachs CEO David Solomon just came out endorsing the CLARITY Act, along with Fidelity, BlackRock, and a bunch of other major financial organizations.
insights.locator: And don’t take it from me

themes.theme: Banks' own blockchain adoption and disintermediation

insights.claim: Every major bank, including JPMorgan, reportedly has significant blockchain deployments already live or set to go live at scale, moving well past experimental pilots, contingent on greater regulatory clarity from CLARITY passage.
insights.speaker: a16z crypto editorial
insights.so_what: Suggests a wave of institutional blockchain product launches is queued behind CLARITY passage — a catalyst investors should watch for as a near-term unlock rather than a multi-year hypothetical.
insights.quote: We’re way past the point where enterprises dip their toe into new technology and do experimental stuff.
insights.locator: But as far as I know, every big bank

insights.claim: Much of the traditional banking system still runs on antiquated COBOL codebases that are too intertwined across institutions to upgrade unilaterally; blockchains offer a shared, unified framework that solves this as a coordination problem, not just a technology problem.
insights.speaker: a16z crypto editorial
insights.so_what: Reframes blockchain adoption in finance as solving an inter-bank coordination failure — implies the addressable market is the entire legacy correspondent-banking stack, not just crypto-native niches.
insights.quote: It’s a joke in Silicon Valley that banks still have COBOL programmers, but it’s actually true.
insights.locator: In their defense, the systems are so intertwined

insights.claim: Blockchains are described as 'disintermediation machines' that remove layers of mediation from money movement, illustrated by an a16z portfolio company international wire transfer that took two weeks to locate because there is no single global wire network, only a patchwork of banks passing paper records to each other.
insights.speaker: a16z crypto editorial
insights.so_what: A concrete first-hand example of legacy cross-border payment fragility that quantifies the pain point stablecoins solve — useful evidence when pitching stablecoin infrastructure investments.
insights.quote: We had a case where we funded an international portfolio company. Two weeks later, we couldn’t find the money.
insights.locator: The other thing I’ll say is that the simple way

insights.claim: Sending remittances to Mexico through traditional channels currently costs 8-10% in fees, versus near-zero cost via stablecoins because no intermediary sits in the middle of the transaction.
insights.speaker: a16z crypto editorial
insights.so_what: A specific, quantified cost-reduction figure (8-10% to near-zero) that makes the stablecoin remittance thesis concrete and testable against real market data.
insights.quote: If you send money to Mexico right now using, they charge 8 to 10 percent. With a stablecoin, it’s almost zero.
insights.locator: I can send you a dollar with no intermediary

themes.theme: Developer liability as an existential threat

insights.claim: Imposing unlimited downstream liability on software developers for how third parties later misuse their software is described as a 'kill shot' to the industry, since developers cannot anticipate all future uses of general-purpose products — analogized to holding a hotel owner liable for a guest's crime or a car engineer liable for a robbery getaway.
insights.speaker: a16z crypto editorial
insights.so_what: Identifies developer-liability rules as a distinct existential policy risk to both crypto and AI open-source ecosystems, separate from the market-structure debate — a risk factor to monitor in parallel state/federal AI legislation.
insights.quote: It’s a kill shot to the industry. It’s impossible.
insights.locator: Marc: It’s a kill shot to the industry

insights.claim: A clear legal line is drawn between building open, general-purpose software (protected) and knowingly assisting a specific crime (not protected, and already illegal) — courts have reportedly conflated these in some cases.
insights.speaker: a16z crypto editorial
insights.so_what: Gives a workable legal test (intent/knowing assistance vs. general-purpose tool-building) that investors can apply to assess liability exposure in crypto and AI portfolio companies.
insights.quote: If you build a piece of software and say, ‘Hey, criminals, come use it,’... that is a crime.
insights.locator: Chris: And just to add to that

insights.claim: Unlimited downstream liability would specifically kill open-source development first (developers aren't paid and can't absorb liability or insure against it), which cascades to killing academic computer-science research (dependent on open source), then venture investing, then startups, then even large companies.
insights.speaker: a16z crypto editorial
insights.so_what: Lays out an explicit causal chain (open source -> academic CS research -> VC -> startups -> incumbents) that quantifies how far-reaching liability legislation could be for both crypto and AI investment theses if adopted broadly.
insights.quote: So open source dies. Because open source dies, academic research dies... It kills computer science as a field... Then it kills venture investing.
insights.locator: Even if insurance were available to cover unlimited downstream liability

insights.claim: Similar unlimited-downstream-liability bills have been proposed for AI models, including in California, and nearly passed; Andreessen states plainly he believes proponents of such liability rules are deliberately trying to kill the industry rather than acting from a misunderstanding.
insights.speaker: a16z crypto editorial
insights.so_what: Directly ties the crypto developer-liability fight to ongoing AI regulation battles, implying the same lobbying/policy playbook and stakes apply across both a16z's core investment sectors.
insights.quote: I think they’re deliberately trying to kill the industry.
insights.locator: Marc: This is the thing. This is a very live issue in AI policy

themes.theme: Securities law and the decentralization threshold

insights.claim: Tokenizing an existing security (e.g., a stock) does not exempt it from SEC oversight under the CLARITY Act — it remains a security and is regulated as such; the bill only clarifies treatment for newly created tokens.
insights.speaker: a16z crypto editorial
insights.so_what: Directly rebuts a common bear-case narrative that CLARITY would let companies 'launder' securities out of SEC jurisdiction by tokenizing them — important for compliance risk assessment.
insights.quote: If you take a stock and tokenize it, that’s a security, and it’s regulated by the SEC like a security.
insights.locator: Chris: No. This is in the bill.

insights.claim: The CLARITY Act codifies a decentralization-threshold framework: new tokens start under SEC regulation (as securities, with lockups and disclosure) while centrally controlled, then transition to CFTC regulation (as commodities, like Bitcoin and Ethereum today) once they cross a defined decentralization threshold with no central actor holding inside information or control.
insights.speaker: a16z crypto editorial
insights.so_what: This is the core legal mechanism of the bill — investors need this threshold concept to assess when/how a given token's regulatory classification (and therefore VC lockup exposure) will change over its lifecycle.
insights.quote: Over time, when you hit certain thresholds of decentralization, it starts to look more like Bitcoin or Ethereum today.
insights.locator: The way the CLARITY Act works, at that point, the token is regulated by the SEC

insights.claim: The prior administration's agencies and courts had already implicitly treated Bitcoin and Ethereum as sufficiently decentralized to be regulated as commodities over the past decade; CLARITY does not create new doctrine but hard-codes existing consensus into statute.
insights.speaker: a16z crypto editorial
insights.so_what: Suggests the bill's core classification framework is lower political/legal risk than critics claim, since it formalizes rather than invents the current regulatory status quo.
insights.quote: This has been implicit in court cases and agency decisions from both parties for the last 10 years.
insights.locator: Even the last administration implicitly agreed with this framework

insights.claim: If CLARITY passes, a16z's effective lockup period on tokens it invests in will lengthen significantly, since venture capitalists and founders face lockups until a project's token meets the 'sufficient decentralization' criteria.
insights.speaker: a16z crypto editorial
insights.so_what: A direct, self-disclosed disclosure of how the bill affects a16z's own fund liquidity/exit timelines — material for anyone modeling VC-token liquidity dynamics post-CLARITY.
insights.quote: If the CLARITY Act passes, our effective lockup period — the period in which we can sell — will increase significantly.
insights.locator: There are no rules for insider trading or lockups

themes.theme: If CLARITY fails, and the regulation-vs-innovation framing

insights.claim: If the CLARITY Act does not pass, agencies (SEC, CFTC, Treasury) can still implement pieces of the framework administratively, but agency rulemaking lacks the durability of legislation, prolonging regulatory uncertainty and discouraging long-horizon investment and building.
insights.speaker: a16z crypto editorial
insights.so_what: Sets expectations for a fallback scenario: even without CLARITY, incremental agency-level progress is likely, but with materially less investment certainty than statute would provide.
insights.quote: The big difference is that legislation is de facto permanent in a way that agency rulemaking is not.
insights.locator: Number two, a lot of these things can be and are being done

insights.claim: Andreessen coins/uses the term 'anarcho-tyranny' — a government that lets rule-breakers act with impunity while regulating/prosecuting law-abiding actors to death — to describe the 2020-2024 U.S. crypto policy regime, contrasted with the 'Goldilocks' middle-ground regulatory approach CLARITY represents.
insights.speaker: a16z crypto editorial
insights.so_what: A reusable political-economy framework for evaluating regulatory regimes generally (not just crypto) — useful lens for assessing policy risk across a16z's other regulated sectors like AI.
insights.quote: Anarcho-tyranny is essentially a government in which you regulate law-abiding people to death.
insights.locator: Marc: Political theorists talk about all the different forms of government

insights.claim: Under the 2020-2024 anarcho-tyranny regime, startups outside the U.S. operated freely (leading to FTX) while U.S.-based startups were 'brutally punished' with no legal path to operate — illustrating that excessive domestic enforcement without corresponding rules pushed risk offshore rather than eliminating it.
insights.speaker: a16z crypto editorial
insights.so_what: Reinforces the thesis that prosecutorial-only policy doesn't reduce industry risk, it relocates it to less accountable jurisdictions — a durable lesson applicable to future tech policy debates (e.g., AI).
insights.quote: Startups outside the U.S. went wild and did whatever they wanted, which, as we discussed, led to FTX.
insights.locator: That was the governance regime under the prior administration

themes.theme: American technology leadership and long-term crypto vision

insights.claim: Every American citizen, regardless of political position, should want the U.S. to remain the global technology leader because it delivers direct economic wealth, national-security advantages (easier for agencies like the FBI to deal with domestic companies), and career/educational opportunities for American kids that have persisted for a hundred years.
insights.speaker: a16z crypto editorial
insights.so_what: States the top-level strategic argument a16z uses to frame crypto policy as a national-competitiveness issue, not merely an industry lobbying position — relevant for understanding the firm's broader policy advocacy playbook.
insights.quote: We always make a very strong argument on this: every American citizen, regardless of political position, should want America to be the technology leader in the world.
insights.locator: Marc: We would argue this is in the long tradition

insights.claim: For the next couple of years post-CLARITY, the dominant crypto use case will remain financial ('finance 2.0'): stablecoins, tokenized stocks, bonds, Treasury bills, and lending, extending high-functioning U.S.-style financial infrastructure globally.
insights.speaker: a16z crypto editorial
insights.so_what: Gives investors a near-term sector-allocation signal within crypto: financial-infrastructure and tokenization plays are the highest-conviction near-term opportunity versus more speculative long-tail use cases.
insights.quote: I think that will be the dominant use case in the next couple of years.
insights.locator: The use cases that have worked so far have been financial

insights.claim: Longer-term, if AI agents proliferate as expected, crypto assets are predicted to be the natural medium for an internet of billions/trillions of AI agents conducting autonomous economic transactions with each other.
insights.speaker: a16z crypto editorial
insights.so_what: A speculative but strategically important long-horizon thesis linking crypto rails directly to AI-agent economies — a thematic convergence point for investors positioning across both AI and crypto portfolios.
insights.quote: There could be an internet of billions and trillions of AI agents conducting economic transactions. The natural way they would do that would be through crypto assets.
insights.locator: Longer-term, as I talk about in my book

insights.claim: Beyond finance and AI-agent payments, further-future use cases floated include creative-industry services, social networks, and games built on blockchain rails.
insights.speaker: a16z crypto editorial
insights.so_what: Marks additional, lower-conviction long-tail verticals worth monitoring for early-stage blockchain-native startups once the finance 2.0 wave matures.
insights.quote: You can also imagine all sorts of other future use cases, which I allude to at the end of my book: services for creative people, social networks, games, and more.
insights.locator: Longer-term, as I talk about in my book
